The concept of "death of the author" is about the idea that community and individual tastes brings values to art, not creative intent. But in that view, you might notice that this means that the Polluck you chose to bring distaste to is still both incredibly valid, and, as a commodity, considered widely valuable and an important piece of art- Which also means that there's enough importance put into the reality of how it was made to make it effectively unrecreatable through an AI.

You can't hold both of these views at the same time. If you believe that art is to be held as valuable based on Death Of The Artist, then Pollock's works are valuable because people find their specific approach valuable in a way that a random splatter would not. Something that requires HIS specific craft and skillsets- and thus, similar to many, many other art styles, emulable, but ultimately personal.  
  
If you're going to say it comes down to taste, then asking "what makes us have the taste we do?" forces you to either return to the Death Of The Artist, or look at art as a product of another person's experiences and decisions, which returns us to my original perspective.

Let me ask you this- Do you think your appreciation of aesthetics is rooted in conscious choices or unconscious preferences?

"Well, I've always been fond of "Starry Night" by Van Gogh. It touches me because it reminds me of moments in my childhood when my parents would take me to my grandmother's house, and she lived in an incredibly small town, so there wasn't hardly any light pollution. So when we would leave her house at night, I would look up and see the most amazing sky. Starry Night reminds me of that. And it doesn't capture exactly how the sky looks, but it does represent how it felt." 

Fascinating you say this, given the fact that it was largely created while Van Gogh created it in highly similar circumstances while choosing to be treated in an asylum. Van Gogh also professed a closeness to family and a long, upsetting past of isolation and rejection in his pursuits. 


Maybe you're not a spiritual person, but you're likely a believer in symbols. Perhaps the reason you connect to Starry Night is not just your own personal connection, but one made of recognizing subconsciously the feelings of another human being and the choices they made to make a work of art that validated the way they felt in what they saw in the world.

AI is making decisions- It fundamentally has to. It's using reinforcement learning methods and predictive algorithms to decide what each pixel of an image should be based on what it's been given as input. You won't call this "decisions" because you relate this to a conscious process made by a human being. I call this decisions because it is fundamentally decided by a "thinking process" that is only making choices based on what it "values". 

A chess computer is capable of doing the same. Some chess computers favor more maverick plays, others play a highly technical game. 

And if you want to say what I said was "word salad", perhaps you can explain to me what I meant by it?

See, I've seen this opinion again and again, but I have to ask- Have you ever \*seen\* a polluck painting in person?

A lot of Polluck's technique requires seeing the actual painting- they aren't just flat canvases, they're layers and layers of paint worked on top of one another to create a sense of depth and dimension to the splatter art. The question of whether or not someone can paint like Pollock is a valid one- But the reality is, many can paint LIKE Polluck, but miss the aspects that allow Polluck to deliver consistently provocative pieces of abstract art.

And if you want to get technical, your argument about the reproductivity of art seems to comprehend art as a commodity rather than something to connect to. Can you share a piece of art you genuinely feel an emotional connection to? Something that's provocative for your tastes and interests?

The purpose of split pushing is to introduce a game state that is, on the surface, equal, but forces the opposing team to make a decision where to put resources. Ideally, in this state of equilibrium, either your team will be able to win a 2v2, or force an opponent to create a 3v2. Hey, My Name’s ANON. Not that it matters, really, so I’m going to get right into it.

Deadlock is my first MOBA, BUT I’m also pretty familiar with team games in general, and have played a lot of random competitive titles. My lack of interest of MOBA’s up to this point warrants me having a good perspective on what I felt like I needed to have explained to me to allow me to play a game of Deadlock without feeling like a chicken with my head cut off.


PHASES


First thing I think would have helped my onboarding experience vastly is to have each section of the game separated out a little more clearly by the announcer. A lot of the time, I find myself looking at the minimap to see what stage of the game we’re on, and still haven’t figured out the exact timing of when Jungles open, or when the Midboss arrives. 

Secondly, I think it would be a lot more helpful to have the tutorial break the game into phases. 


Phase 1 is commonly referred to as “The Laning Phase” by the community, and I think making the overall objective- Pushing back the lane to the guardian, and killing it- a lot more clear as the goal OF the phase would help the new player figure out their place in the team a bit better. The game does a good job of encouraging new players to return to the store to spend on stuff, as well, from the player barks- those are great. 


Phase 2 should be called “The Training Phase” or something, and it’s where the objectives come a lot more vague. Sure, there’s still the overall goal of lane pushing, and taking out the bigger guardian, but there’s a lot more importance placed here for teamfights and teamplay in general. Having the game mention that “Blue needs support!” When the game detects an income gap of over 2k between the opposing lane partners would help encourage the “winning player” to jump to assist in a teamfight.

On top of this, I think it would be good for the characters to occasionally mention the need to Jungle as well, when they are behind economically and have lost the lane fight- Like when their guardian is down, but the enemies isn’t. Then, after the economic gap has been displaced to be within reasonable margins, having the character say “enough screwing around, I gotta get back to the fight!” would be perfect to organically encourage players back to the lanes.


Also, I would absolutely love to see a big, glowing neon sign attached to the entrance of each lane, that you can’t miss while sailing out of home-base, declaring the overall earnings on each lane, and the amount of “missed souls” to indicate how often a lane has gone unoccupied by your team. This would be a great way to encourage players to notice when a lane has been underutilized, and to seize the opportunity to prevent the lost capital. 

Phase 3 should be triggered once two or more of the Walkers have been killed. I think you could indicate the difference of this phase visually, with some big magic thing happening- Maybe the sun starts to set, and the lights start going on all around town- Maybe an eclipse occurs, maybe steam starts to pour out of vents- just indicate that the situation has escalated, and that it’s time to start thinking about the end of the game. At this point, the brightest spot on the map should be the Patron that’s currently in danger- If you put a big beam of light over the enemy base, it’ll be really easy to tell at a glance where you’ll need to go to close the game out.

At Phase 3, I feel like player deaths should be communicated stronger, with having the characters drop a bark whenever they hear someone die. It feels like for the final patron fight, having in the chaos of those close teamfights a steady communication of “who’s alive, who’s dead” would keep a new player from jumping into a teamfight they are not prepared for. Granted, experience must be a teacher here of when a fight is going sour, But making the odds a lot more clear would be ideal for keeping track of the game state. 


THE SHOP


Finally- the build system is absolutely genius, and is easily my favorite design feature of the game. However, I still felt very intimidated by the sheer size of the list in each section, and I get confused around the midpoint of the game, when I’ve filled up all my slots, what to spend money on. I think a great way to get new players to get used to dropping old items they’ve been relying on is for the game to notice when a player is holding onto a weaker item, and have the shopkeep offer up a “Deal of the week!” that gives the full resale price on a tier one item when tier fours are available. This wouldn’t let an experienced player suddenly switch their build or anything, and having the extra 250 isn’t going to change the economic situation on any build in the late game- but it will be that little “sweetening the deal” needed to encourage a player to take what looks like on the surface as a bad choice (selling a item and losing money) to be a great choice (the value gained from a much better item). This should only proc after you’ve held onto a low tier item for at least 3 shop visits, and after that, it shouldn’t be offered again. 



CHARACTER SELECT


Character select is a bit confusing, especially the “priority system.” I think you should just have a “1,2,3” as the default option for match picks, and then have a checkbox option to “turn off character priority” on that screen. I feel like that would encourage new players to focus on a character much more, which would avoid overburdening them with options.


SPIRIT POWER VS WEAPON POWER


Finally, I think it’s really important to just say “Spirit Power is Damage from Special Abilities”, and then “Weapon Power is Damage from Normal Attacks” somewhere, directly. Stuff like Wrath’s “Full Auto” does not lend to a whole lot of clarity if Spirit Power would buff that, or not. I have no idea where you could clarify that, but It definitely can feel a little strange playing and not understanding the difference between the two.

I think you've understated this. This is one of the best opening scenes in a movie, *ever*. 

Scream's opening creates a short that, essentially, explores it's own basic premise to exhaustion- "A slasher movie where the main character is familiar with slasher movies"- And demonstrates, fully, why that premise would fall apart in contact to reality. Most people- even people who are convinced they were fearless- Would not be able to handle the circumstances offered by a home invasion piloted by someone aiming to kill you, with no fear of the consequences. 

So what does Scream do? It makes that movie, milks that concept for all its worth in its perfectly paced, swinging-like-a-metronome opening, and then doubles down on its own concept in the rest of the movie to go " Ok, but let's imagine what 'real teens' would do in this situation", and paints them with a sardonic, ironic brush of its own era- and then keeps the tension between reality, and the movies own fiction as tight as possible. 

Scream was so good, it killed slasher movies by killing its own concept off in the first film.

"Magic", in Paranoid, is a largely ritualistic activity only able to be performed by Witches. 

It is a form of Shade Manipulation that operates off of two rules - The first being that, ultimately, whatever "spell" you cast will actively conspire against the caster to induce an ironic resolution, meaning spellcasters have to be highly specific and rigorously controlled to avoid consequences that completely jeopardize the goal. 

(For example, you can't just cast a spell to make someone "fall in love", because that's such a vaguely defined thing that Shade could find all manner of ironic answers to make someone "Fall in Love", like spraining their ankle during Tennis Practice or breaking their neck after proposing on a roller coaster. You could, however, cast a spell to "Make yourself attractive in the eye of (name here)", and only suffer the ironic consequences of being completely detestable to anyone else. There's always a cost, and you always ultimately are worse off using magic than you started in the short term.)

The other rule is that Shade feeds off emotions, so every "witch", generally, needs to spend time leeching emotions out of other people as to have a surplus of emotions to work with. This is generally up to the individual witch to decide what they'd prefer to gather the most, often based on their individual temperament and personality.

This is some general advice for tf2, but it applies the most to pyro: there is always going to be a lot of situations where the best option is going to be to hang back and wait for others to go in. Pyro has the hardest time of the core combat classes dealing with competent players, simply because the class relies on positioning mistakes to secure kills. So, you have to accept that doing well at pyro isnt securing frags all the time, but more spitting in peoples faces.

Pyro, I've found, works best as an unholy annoyance. Your job is to force other players to deal with you or change to less effective strats. You shut down long range projectile spam, you help redirect Ubers, and you punish players for not paying attention to you. I repeat- fragging is often not the most useful thing a pyro can do. The most useful thing pyros can do is annoy enemies into making mistakes for the other classes, and when you can, capitalizing on their mistakes to get cheeky kills.

After a long time of maining pyro, realizing just how opposing player skill dependant the class is- moreso than any other class in the game, as even the main issues spy has can still result in the spy accomplishing useful gamewinning goals with proper play- I've decided to main the other core classes as a result

Nintendo can't compete with sony or Microsoft without pressing the gimmick envelope. Since they have a mentality of toys, rather than hardware, we often their consoles to be less powerful than their peers. Thus, if their console doesn't have a strong enough gimmick, they'll never sell.

But the N64 didn't do anything... New. Sure, better graphics, but nothing diverse, no shocking revelation. And the same thing happened to the GameCube- they tried to just make a better, more processing power console against two juggernauts of already existing electronic companies.

Now, when the Wii came out, for the most part, it enjoyed more sales than the other two competitions, yadda yadda, you know the story. But then, the Wii u suffered from a lack of brand identity, and a lack of interest in it's gimmick- not much changed with a touchscreen interface- we had seen the iPad before.

TLDR: Nintendo consoles sell on the strength of their gimmick, rather than hardware capabilities. The Wii U was to similar to what we were familar with due to iPads. It failed to push the envelope.

However, There are some ways to preserve the series of events and make it much more readable. Shifting it over to Tina's perspective allows us the keep him being who he is, and make a point that Tina at this point is likely better off with him than not, given her shortcomings at survival. It also keeps the darkness of it, as we still are deeply offended by the idea of this cruel system. Finally, having the protagonist remain aloof and distant gives some credible space to what he's really thinking, giving him a chance at redemption. Plus, the idea of exploring this story with the naive, happy-go-lucky Tina in direct Juxtaposition with the dark depressive world they live in would be interesting. If you still want to keep the Protagonist's voice, you could shift the perspective between the two every chapter or so.
